title: Implement least-privilege access with designations in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: SageMaker Unified Studio adds designations: named permission sets assigned to project members so engineers, stewards, analysts and ML users get different rights in one project.
Manageable from console, CLI and CloudFormation at no extra cost.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS IAM Identity Center
decision: One shared project with role-based designations vs separate projects per persona

title: Optimizing Apache HBase availability on Amazon EMR, Part 1: Coordinator startup, RegionServer recovery, and regions in transition
key_points: A three-level triage process for HBase on EMR: slow-starting coordinator, RegionServers dropping out, and regions stuck in transition.
Maps each symptom to the UI pages, commands and log lines that reveal the cause.
authors: Reekunj Parmar, Ishan Sharma, Ram Nethi

title: Introducing time series collections for the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
key_points: OpenSearch Serverless gets time-series collections for logs, metrics and traces, scaling compute with ingest spikes and down to zero.
Recent data stays hot, older data stays queryable cheaply; alerting and anomaly detection are included.

title: From Problem to Fix in Minutes: Automating Search Relevance Tuning with the Amazon OpenSearch Service Relevance Agent
key_points: An agent inside the OpenSearch UI reads user-behaviour data, forms a hypothesis about poor search ranking, tests it offline and proposes a better query.
Follow-up to an earlier post on measuring search quality.
authors: Aruna Govindaraju, Sean Bjurstrom, Mingshi Liu

title: Enable cross-Region fine-grained data access with AWS Lake Formation and Trusted Identity Propagation
key_points: Trusted Identity Propagation carries the signed-in user's identity through the query engine to Lake Formation, so access rules and CloudTrail logs apply per person, not per shared IAM role.
Identity Center can now replicate identities to other Regions, so data shared from one Region can be queried as the same user in another.
Shows it for S3 data via Athena and for Redshift data via a Glue federated catalog; part 1 of 3.
services: AWS Lake Formation, AWS IAM Identity Center, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
decision: Shared IAM role vs per-user identity propagation for auditable fine-grained access across accounts and Regions
authors: Maneesh Sharma, Laura Reith, Sri Pooja Ravipati, Songzhi Liu

title: Build RAG-ready indexes from Amazon S3 with Amazon OpenSearch intelligent ingestion
key_points: New managed ingestion in OpenSearch Serverless turns documents in S3 into a vector index: it parses, describes images, chunks, embeds and indexes without a pipeline to build.
One-off ingestion jobs or continuous streams that keep the index in sync with the bucket.
decision: Managed document ingestion vs self-built parse/chunk/embed pipeline for RAG

title: Trace security threats in multi-agent pipelines with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Instruments a multi-agent LLM pipeline so prompt-injection paths and cross-tenant PII leaks can be traced in OpenSearch.
Core advice: log the hops between agents, distrust tool calls whose lineage touches untrusted content, and tag PII by origin.

title: dbt and Amazon Redshift Data Sharing: Multi-cluster pipelines without moving a byte
key_points: Shares live tables from a producer Redshift warehouse to a consumer (same or other account/Region) with a datashare, so no copy pipeline is needed.
dbt runs on the consumer, declares the shared database as a source, and builds staging and reporting models on top of it.
Walkthrough uses dbt Cloud, but the source/model pattern applies equally to dbt Core.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift data sharing, Amazon Redshift Serverless, dbt
decision: Copy data between warehouses with ETL vs live data sharing; whether dbt runs on the producer or consumer side

title: Resolving concurrent write conflicts for Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon Redshift
key_points: Iceberg's optimistic concurrency rejects a commit whenever the table version moved, even if the two writers touched different data.
Redshift now checks for real overlap at operation, then partition, then file level, and commits writes that don't actually collide.
Includes a system view to see how conflicts were resolved.
decision: Serialize writers vs partition around conflicts vs rely on engine-level conflict resolution for concurrent Iceberg writes
authors: Sanjay Devireddy, Madhukiran vaddi, Srishti Mittal, Xiening Dai

title: Build cross-account streaming pipelines with the Amazon Kinesis Producer Library and Kinesis Client Library
key_points: Lays out the topologies for producing to and consuming from Kinesis across AWS accounts, then builds the strictest one: producer, stream and consumer each in their own account.
Kinesis resource policies replace IAM role chaining for cross-account access; KMS keys and monitoring still need coordinating.
Lists common cross-account errors and what changed in recent KPL/KCL versions.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, KPL / KCL, AWS IAM, AWS KMS, Amazon DynamoDB
decision: Which account owns the stream: producer-side, consumer-side or a separate stream account
attaches_to: aws-bytes: real-time streaming (later); links to S3 cross-account migration (done)
authors: Charishma Makineni, Chinmayi Narasimhadevara, Pratik Patel, Priyanka Chaudhary

title: Bring data quality to your Amazon EMR workloads with Amazon EMR Data Quality built on AWS Glue Data Quality
key_points: Glue's DQDL rules now run natively inside EMR Spark jobs, removing the choice between hand-rolled Deequ checks and routing data through Glue.
Two patterns: a quick inline check, and Iceberg write-audit-publish where data lands on a branch and merges only if it passes a managed ruleset.
Works on all three EMR deployment modes.
services: Amazon EMR, AWS Glue Data Quality, Apache Iceberg
decision: Where data-quality checks run: Deequ vs Glue DQ vs in-engine DQDL vs dbt tests; plain write vs write-audit-publish
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Data Quality Check (done) - follow-up angle
authors: Mert Hocanin, Aditya Vallabhani, Edison Xie, Shrey Malpani, Linan Zheng

title: Query across accounts and table formats with multi-catalog in Amazon EMR
key_points: Spark normally allows one catalog extension per session, so mixing Iceberg, Delta, Hudi and Hive tables, or reaching other accounts' Glue catalogs, needed workarounds.
EMR 8.1 adds an opt-in catalog that detects each table's format from Glue metadata and routes the query, including across accounts without copying data.
Works on EMR Serverless, EC2 and EKS.
services: Amazon EMR, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi
decision: One routing catalog vs per-format catalogs / Lake Formation shares for multi-format, multi-account data mesh

title: Monitoring MWAA-orchestrated ETL pipelines with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Streams CloudWatch logs from Airflow DAGs, Glue jobs and EC2 scripts into OpenSearch so one pipeline failure can be traced in one place.
An OpenSearch MCP server on Bedrock AgentCore lets an agent find the root cause and suggest a fix.
Deployed as three CloudFormation stacks plus a SageMaker notebook.
services: Amazon MWAA, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS Glue
decision: Per-service CloudWatch log groups vs centralised log search for multi-service ETL failures
authors: Anupa Bhattacharyya, Sean Bjurstrom, Manikandan Mylsamy, Karthik Seshadri

title: Cost-effective ETL with DuckDB and Amazon S3 Tables on AWS Glue
key_points: DuckDB can run inside a normal Glue 6.0 Python job, read Parquet from S3 and commit Iceberg snapshots straight to S3 Tables via the REST catalog.
Meant for small, SQL-only, frequent jobs where Spark's startup and cluster overhead dominate; Spark stays the choice for distributed work.
Includes a side-by-side cost/runtime comparison against Spark on the same runtime; AWS reports Glue 6.0 is 30% cheaper than earlier versions.
services: AWS Glue, Amazon S3 Tables, DuckDB, Apache Iceberg
decision: DuckDB vs Spark (vs Athena CTAS / Lambda) for small daily ETL

title: Run an automated operational review with the Amazon Redshift MCP server
key_points: A review_cluster tool in the Redshift MCP server runs the usual health-check queries (table design, WLM, long queries, sizing) and turns them into a prioritised findings report.
Driven from Kiro in plain language; needs only the sys:monitor role.
AWS reports a manual review usually takes 4–8 hours per cluster.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift MCP server, Kiro
decision: Periodic manual Redshift health review vs agent-driven review
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (run the review on the Redshift Serverless workgroup)
authors: Sidhanth Muralidhar, Sergey Konoplev, Vlad Siniavin

title: Materialize once, query anywhere: Introducing Iceberg materialized views in Amazon Redshift
key_points: Redshift can now store a materialized view as an Iceberg table in S3 / S3 Tables, registered in Glue, so Athena, EMR and Glue read the same precomputed result.
Refresh stays incremental and is done by Redshift; the result is governed like any catalog table (IAM or Lake Formation).
Pitched for medallion layers, feature stores and cutting duplicate compute across engines.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena
decision: Where to materialize shared aggregates: Redshift native MV vs Iceberg MV vs dbt incremental model on Iceberg
authors: Sudipta Bagchi, Andre Hernich, Gaurav Saxena, Dhaval Shah, Srishti Mittal

title: Optimize consumer rebalancing on Amazon MSK with next generation protocol
key_points: The old Kafka rebalance makes every consumer in a group pause, even ones whose partitions don't move; the new KIP-848 protocol moves coordination to the broker and only touches affected consumers.
Available on MSK for Kafka 4.x (Standard and Express); switching needs client config changes and removal of deprecated settings.
Includes a diagnosis path for slow rebalances using broker logs.
decision: Classic/cooperative vs broker-side (KIP-848) rebalancing for large Kafka consumer groups
authors: Yashika Jain, Kalyan Janaki, Vinayaka Gangadhar
